title: Topological Sort
tagline: Order a DAG so every edge points forward — the backbone of scheduling and build systems.

intuition.analogy: Getting dressed: socks before shoes, shirt before jacket. A topological order is any sequence that respects all 'must come before' constraints. There can be several valid orders, but never one that violates a dependency.
paragraphs: A topological sort linearises a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that for every edge u→v, u appears before v. It exists if and only if the graph has no cycles.

Kahn's algorithm builds it greedily by indegree: repeatedly take any node with no remaining prerequisites, output it, and remove its outgoing edges (decrementing neighbours' indegrees). If you can't output all nodes, a cycle exists.

The DFS variant pushes nodes onto a stack on finish (post-order) and reverses it. Both run in linear time and power task scheduling, course planning, build dependency resolution, and DP ordering on DAGs.
intuition.keyIdea: Repeatedly emit a node with zero remaining prerequisites; leftover nodes mean a cycle.

steps.title: Compute indegrees
steps.detail: Count incoming edges for each node. Enqueue all nodes with indegree 0.

steps.title: Peel zero-indegree nodes
steps.detail: Pop a node, append it to the order, and for each neighbour decrement its indegree; enqueue any that hit 0.

steps.title: Cycle check
steps.detail: If the output contains all V nodes, success. Otherwise the remaining nodes form a cycle.

complexity.timeReason: Each node and edge is processed once.

pitfalls: Only DAGs have a topological order — always handle the cycle case.
Multiple valid orders exist; don't assume uniqueness unless indegrees force it.
For lexicographically smallest order, use a min-heap instead of a plain queue.

dryRun.clickMoment: Node 2 only becomes available after BOTH 0 and 1 are emitted (its indegree drops from 2 to 0). The indegree counter is what enforces 'all prerequisites first'.

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.statement: Return a valid course order, or empty if impossible.
problems.hint: Kahn's algorithm; empty output means a cycle.

approach: Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, start a queue with all zero in-degree courses, and repeatedly take a course, appending it to the order and decrementing its successors.
If the produced order has fewer than n courses, a cycle exists → return empty.

problems.title: Alien Dictionary
problems.statement: Infer letter order from sorted alien words.
problems.hint: Build precedence edges from adjacent word comparisons, then topo sort.

approach: Derive ordering constraints by comparing adjacent words: the first differing character gives an edge u → v. Watch the invalid prefix case ("abc" before "ab").
Topologically sort the letters with Kahn's algorithm; a cycle means no valid order.

problems.title: Parallel Courses
problems.statement: Minimum semesters to finish all courses.
problems.hint: Topo sort by layers; the number of layers is the answer.

approach: Each Kahn BFS layer is one semester: all currently unblocked courses can be taken together.
Count layers until the queue empties; if some course never reaches in-degree 0, there is a cycle → -1.

problems.title: Sort Items by Groups
problems.statement: Order items respecting item and group dependencies.
problems.hint: Two-level topological sort (groups, then within groups).

approach: Two-level topological sort: order items within each group, and order the groups among themselves, then concatenate.
Give every group-less item its own group. Build item-edges and group-edges from the before-lists, topo-sort both, then emit each group's items in their internal topo order following the group order.

problems.title: Longest Path in a DAG
problems.statement: Find the longest path in a DAG.

approach: On a DAG the longest path is found by relaxing edges in topological order: process nodes so all predecessors are done first.
dp[v] = max over incoming edges (dp[u] + w). Track the global maximum; topological order guarantees each dp is final when used.
